headline: A lifelong book lover says reading gives her belonging and a break that nothing else gives.
story: Emily has read since she was little: the kid in the corner with a book, reading clubs every summer, a love she got from her grandma.
The turn: reading gives her a sense of belonging, because she can feel with the characters and know she is not alone.
Nothing else takes her out of these walls like books do. It is about what books give her, not what prison takes.

transcript:
--- P1055416.MOV (Emily, WCCW) ---
[00:01] Interviewer: Alright, can you introduce yourself and tell me about your relationship with reading?
[00:07] Interviewee: My name is Emily. I have been reading since I was little. That was my go-to to get away from the world.
[00:16] Interviewee: I was one of those little nerds growing up that you couldn't find me outside, you couldn't find me hiding in my room.
[00:24] Interviewee: It's usually in the corner reading a book. I was an exceptional reader, especially in school. I was reading 3 or 4 grades above my level.
[00:34] Interviewee: I was always in the reading clubs growing up through the summer and even just now. I got it from my grandma.
[00:44] Interviewee: I have all my paper books. I have my Kindle e-reader. I have a regular reader for my Kindle of just my books.
[00:52] Interviewee: I take them with me everywhere. Everybody knows that they need something to read if we're on a trip or something.
[00:59] Interviewee: They just give me something and they know I got it. That's just me. I love to read.
[01:05] Interviewer: Alright, that's great. What did you think when you first heard about the Inside Literary Project?
[01:12] Interviewer: When I first heard about this project, the literary project, I was a little, not necessarily skeptical.
[01:21] Interviewer: I was a little, just like, what is it? What are we going to do? Does this really matter? Is this really something or is it just a small program that the campus is putting on?
[01:33] Interviewee: Then I went to the first meeting and I was just like, oh, this is actually something that is important. I actually can have a voice in this. This is really cool.
[01:41] Interviewee: It was pretty inspiring to go to that first meeting and actually know what action was going to take place.
[01:49] Interviewer: Absolutely. What qualities make a book stand out to you as a judge?
[01:55] Interviewee: Qualities that stand out to me in a book that are important, I feel like, is being able to capture the reader, especially in the first couple pages.
[02:07] Interviewee: Whether it is pulling on emotions, whether it's sad or happy, being able to incorporate humor sometimes, like how they were talking about today and the martyr.
[02:18] Interviewee: It can be a serious topic. It can be something that needs to be addressed, but being able to relay that in a way that most people can understand.
[02:28] Interviewee: Whether it's through humor, whether it's through just reaching out and just having an open conversation, but more it's not too heavy.
[02:37] Interviewee: Then being able to wrap it up is a big thing because there's some stories you don't get a good ending to.
[02:45] Interviewee: Having an ending that you can either interpret yourself or that is just a point like this is a good ending, those are some key qualities for me.
[02:59] Interviewer: How does being a judge make you feel about your role as a reader?
[03:04] Interviewee: Being a judge for this, as a role for being a reader, it makes me feel, I don't know, it's important.
[03:14] Interviewee: It makes me want to read more and more genres, not just the kind that I typically prefer.
[03:20] Interviewee: Honestly, most of these books probably weren't something I might have just picked off the shelf, but even just through the discussions that we've had, I really enjoyed them.
[03:31] Interviewee: It's opened my mind a lot to different things than just a set type of book that I'm going to read now.
[03:41] Interviewer: Absolutely. Why is it important that incarcerated people are part of literary conversation?
[03:49] Interviewee: I believe it's important for us as incarcerated people to be part of these conversations.
[03:55] Interviewee: It gives us a voice. Being incarcerated, reading is a big part of our day.
[04:03] Interviewee: It takes us outside of the walls that we're in here.
[04:06] Interviewee: So being able to be a part of that and to have a say in not necessarily what is coming in, but what is being advertised or pushed or promoted,
[04:19] Interviewee: helps us feel like we get to be a part of something that is changing our communities too, on the outside, not just in here.
[04:32] Interviewer: Have you read all five books?
[04:33] Interviewee: No, I have not read all five books yet. I wish.
[04:41] Interviewer: What does reading give you that nothing else does?
[04:46] Interviewee: Reading gives me a sense of belonging in a way that nothing else really does, because I can empathize with the characters.
[04:59] Interviewee: Sometimes people are too scared to open up about their own traumas that they've gone through or experiences that they've gone through.
[05:06] Interviewee: You can read all about that. It not necessarily normalizes it, but it makes you feel like you're not alone.
[05:14] Interviewee: You're included in different aspects of life.
[05:17] Interviewee: It also just takes me out. Nothing else takes me out of these walls like books do.
[05:22] Interviewee: It just gives me a break from life, sometimes from reality. That's what it does.
[05:30] Interviewee: Absolutely. Thank you.
[05:32] Interviewee: Thanks so much, Emily.
